strapline: The Fund says yes in principle, bus fares follow the fuel, and the prayer day moves to December

stories.title: The Fund says yes in principle: a US$1.47 billion staff-level deal — now come the prior actions
stories.excerpt: Zambia and the IMF have reached a staff-level agreement on a 36-month, US$1.472 billion Extended Credit Facility. Board approval and a set of prior actions still stand between Friday's handshake and the first disbursement.

image.label: The Fund's answer
image.caption: Zambia and the IMF have a staff-level agreement; board approval and prior actions come next.

body: Zambia has reached a staff-level agreement with the International Monetary Fund on a new US$1.472 billion programme, Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane said on Friday, closing a week of negotiations in Lusaka and opening the path to the country's next IMF-supported programme.

The proposed 36-month arrangement, equivalent to **SDR 1.076 billion**, would support the budget and the balance of payments while safeguarding debt sustainability, Dr Musokotwane said. He was flanked at the briefing by Bank of Zambia Governor Denny Kalyalya and, per Mwebantu's report, IMF mission chief Mercedes Vera Martin. The agreement remains subject to approval by IMF management and the Executive Board, and to the completion of prior actions by the Government.

The Fund's statement, carried by Reuters, said the arrangement would support Zambia's efforts to safeguard macroeconomic stability and debt sustainability as well as its balance-of-payments and fiscal financing needs. The previous US$1.7 billion programme — credited with helping Zambia emerge from the debt crisis that followed its 2020 default, Africa's first of the pandemic era — expired in January.

body.text: The numbers the Fund will hold Zambia to

body: The IMF projects the economy to grow **5.6 percent in 2026**, driven by agriculture, mining and exports. Annual inflation fell to 6.1 percent in September, inside the Government's 6-to-8-percent target band, and international reserves have risen to about US$6.1 billion.

Under the programme, the Government plans to raise the primary fiscal surplus progressively to **3 percent of GDP by 2029**, starting in 2027, through stronger revenue mobilisation, improved tax compliance, rationalised exemptions and more efficient spending. Reforms would also tighten oversight of the Food Reserve Agency, state-owned enterprises and public-private partnerships, improve debt management, and clear payment and value-added-tax refund arrears while protecting social spending.

body.text: We have stabilized the economy. We must now grow it.
body.attribution: Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane, at Friday's briefing in Lusaka, quoted by Mwebantu

body: Dr Musokotwane said the goal was not simply to secure an IMF programme but to build an economy measured by jobs, stronger businesses, opportunities for young people, reliable electricity, better public services and higher household incomes. The programme would support President Hichilema's Grow Zambia agenda, which prioritises investment, production, value addition and exports across agriculture, mining, manufacturing, tourism, energy and infrastructure, and the Government would translate the strategy into specific actions with measurable targets and timelines, with regular public updates.

The timing matters at home. The agreement lands as the Treasury prepares the 2027 budget — the finance ministry said this week that government spending is projected to rise by 7 percent — and it gives that budget an external anchor before it is even tabled.

body.title: The programme at a glance
items: Still to come: IMF management and Executive Board approval, plus prior actions
5.6% — IMF growth projection for 2026; inflation 6.1% in September
3% of GDP — target primary surplus by 2029, from 2027

body.confirmed: A staff-level agreement on a 36-month ECF worth SDR 1.076 billion (about US$1.472 billion) was announced on Friday 9 October, per the Finance Minister's briefing reported by Mwebantu and the IMF statement carried by Reuters via CNBC Africa. The previous US$1.7 billion programme expired in January.
body.unverified: When the Executive Board will vote, and the full list of prior actions Zambia must complete first — neither has been published. The detailed conditionality of the programme is not yet public.

IMF reaches staff-level agreement with Zambia on new credit facility

stories.title: Bus fares follow the fuel: RTSA approves Friday rises — 7 percent intercity, K3.50 inter-mine, K2 on Lusaka locals
stories.excerpt: The Road Transport and Safety Agency has approved higher bus fares across the country with effect from Friday 9 October, three weeks after the fuel pump price jumped by more than K6 a litre.

image.label: The fare board
image.caption: Bus fares rise from Friday, on the back of September's fuel-price increase.

body: Commuters pay more from this weekend. The Road Transport and Safety Agency has approved an upward adjustment of bus fares nationwide, effective Friday 9 October, following a request by the Bus and Taxi Owners Association of Zambia.
The approval was made under Section 107(11) of the Road Traffic Act, Chapter 464 of the Laws of Zambia, as amended by Act No. 8 of 2022, RTSA said in a statement.

body.title: The approved increases
items: Peri-urban routes, Lusaka and other towns — K3.00
Local routes, Copperbelt and other towns — K2.00

body: The agency directed all bus operators to revise their fares accordingly and to display the fare charts in every bus and bus station, and advised passenger-transport operators to adhere to the approved fares.

The adjustment follows the Energy Regulation Board's fuel-price increase of 30 September, which added **K6.17 to a litre of petrol and K6.41 to diesel**. News Diggers reports that petrol moved from K25.29 a litre in September to K31.46 in October, and diesel from K26.86 to K33.27 — rises the ERB attributed to the reinstatement of excise duty after the expiry of the tax waiver, sustained geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, and the depreciation of the kwacha.

The fare rise is the second leg of a squeeze this desk has tracked all month: the excise duty returned to the pump at the start of October, and the bus operators argued their costs had moved with it. RTSA has an agreed pricing model intended to prevent reactionary fare changes in response to marginal fuel movements; this month's fuel jump was anything but marginal.
What commuters actually pay will vary by route and operator, but the fare charts now posted in buses and stations are the reference point — and RTSA has said operators must stick to them.

sources.title: RTSA Approves Bus Fare Hike Effective Today

stories.title: 'If you engage in corruption, you are on your own': the President puts the civil service — and MPs' allowances — on notice
stories.excerpt: Beyond the growth targets, Friday's address to the 14th National Assembly carried a blunt warning to public servants, a rebuke over parliamentary allowances, and a defence of the anti-corruption drive.

image.label: On notice
image.caption: The President warns that delivery, not attendance, will measure the public service.

body: President Hakainde Hichilema used Friday's opening of the First Session of the 14th National Assembly to put the public service on notice, telling civil servants that attendance is not delivery and warning MPs that every allowance has an alternative use.

body.text: The value of the public service can no longer be measured by reporting at 8 hours and knocking off at 17 hours, without measurable deliverables and benefits to our people.
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema, addressing Parliament on Friday 9 October, quoted by Lusaka Times

body: "That does not constitute work. It does not constitute delivery," he added. The Presidential Delivery Unit and the Public Private Dialogue Forum — both created to improve service delivery — will be streamlined to serve the Grow Zambia targets. "After all, they are born out of public resources, so they must be accountable to the public," the President said. More services will move onto ZamPortal and the Government Service Bus, with a promise of fewer administrative barriers and a lower cost of dealing with Government.

body.text: A word for the benches in front of him

body: Some of the sharpest lines were aimed at the MPs themselves. "When we put pressure on the Speaker for more allowances, remember we could use those allowances to keep more kids in school," he said. "Maybe we are already comfortable ourselves. Let's release resources to those who need them the most."

He described the rise in the Constituency Development Fund from K1.6 million to K40 million per constituency as revolutionary, while conceding the fund is not always used well: "All of us in this House must agree that we can do better in effective utilisation of this tool, and it has got no partisanship in it." Protecting the CDF was among the reasons the Government gave for restoring excise duty on fuel this month, alongside free education, school feeding and the Social Cash Transfer.

On corruption, the President was blunt. "We reiterate our position that there will be no sacred cows in the fight against corruption. None. None at all," he said. "As we have stated before, if you engage in corruption, you are on your own." Departing from his text, he added: "When people get prosecuted, they cry isms. Whatever isms are convenient... Public resources belong to the public. Full stop."

News Diggers, reporting the same address, noted the President's call to address what he termed the domestic and toxic environment in the country, and his insistence that progress from the first term is now visible: a stabilised economy, restored order and renewed confidence.

The same week offered a small illustration of the machinery he wants defended. The Anti-Corruption Commission charged a 25-year-old Lusaka taxi driver with one count of corrupt practices, alleging he sent **K5,000 by mobile money** to officers of the Department of National Parks and Wildlife in Nakonde to induce the release of 56 vulturine guineafowl intercepted at Nakonde Bus Station — birds valued at more than K200,000, the ACC's head of corporate communications, Joseph Mwenya, said, per Lusaka Times.

sources.title: “If you engage in corruption, you are on your own”: Hichilema puts civil servants and MPs on notice
HH opens Parley, vows to deal with toxicity in the environment

stories.title: The day after: Kampyongo welcomes the unity call, Britain backs Grow Zambia — with a caveat on opposition space
stories.excerpt: The first responses to Friday's address crossed the aisle and the diplomatic row: an opposition lawmaker preaching peace, a British envoy pledging backing with a condition, and the Vice-President urging the country to move on.

image.label: The day after
image.caption: Opposition, diplomats and government figures respond to Friday's address.

body: The first verdicts on President Hichilema's opening address arrived on Saturday, and the most striking came from the opposition benches. Stephen Kampyongo said the development goals set out in the speech can be reached if Zambians embrace peace and unity — among the first responses from the opposition since the new House sat.

Mr Kampyongo welcomed the President's recognition that divisions must be addressed and a less hostile political environment created, saying meaningful development depends on citizens living together despite their differences, Lusaka Times reported.

The President had closed the address with that appeal. "Without unity, there can be no shared future," he told MPs, and — repeating a line from his inauguration — "Whatever our political choices were, we remain one law-abiding people, bound together by Zambia, and a common destiny." He also acknowledged what he called "the toxicity around here" in the domestic political environment.

body.text: London backs the agenda, with a condition

body: British High Commissioner Rebecca Terzeon said the United Kingdom is ready to work with the Government to promote growth, strengthen trade and attract investment, judging that the address made economic growth the clear focus of the next five years.

body.text: The United Kingdom has been a close partner to Zambia for many years. Zambeef has received support from British investment. There are also UK-backed companies and traders active in sectors such as energy.
body.attribution: British High Commissioner Rebecca Terzeon, quoted by Lusaka Times

body: She pointed to the recent visit by Alastair Long, the UK Trade Commissioner for Africa, who held talks on mining, energy, finance and infrastructure — and who, the Times of Zambia notes, has called Zambia "one of Africa's most exciting investment destinations". But Ms Terzeon paired the backing with a caveat: opposition parties need enough space to operate and hold the Government accountable, democratic institutions should remain independent, transparent and effective, and a free media matters to democracy.

Vice-President W.K. Mutale Nalumango made the Government-side appeal, saying the country must look beyond political differences and that its democratic maturity will be measured by respect for institutions. Moving the vote of thanks, nominated MP Mubita Anakoka urged members to study the speech before debating it.

The new-look House featured in the responses too. Lazarus Hakalebula, a mixed-member proportional-representation MP, welcomed the promised talent-identification programme for the creative sector as a chance for people whose abilities have gone unrecognised. First Lady Mutinta Hichilema said the constitutional reforms brought 20 more women, 15 youths and five persons with disabilities into Parliament. UNFPA's country representative, Anna Holmstrom, welcomed the emphasis on medical-supply chains.

The benchmark the Speaker has already set hangs over all of it: Nelly Mutti has declared the Standing Orders her only political party and the Constitution her only manifesto, and said all laws must be measured against the Grow Zambia targets — the so-called 10-10-5-3-3-1-1-1 agenda of 10,000 megawatts, 10 million tonnes of maize, five million tourists, three million tonnes of copper and US$1 billion in beef exports. MPs take up the President's pronouncements in the House this week, the opposition's first formal chance to answer the unity call.

sources.title: Kampyongo Says Peace And Unity Key To Hichilema's Growth Targets

stories.title: 'A serious betrayal': Sumaili leads the backlash as the 18 October prayer holiday is folded into 29 December
stories.excerpt: A day after the Government moved the National Day of Prayer to a merged December commemoration, the minister who once held the religious-affairs portfolio has condemned the change as a betrayal of Christian believers.

image.label: The moved day
image.caption: The 18 October prayer holiday is folded into a new 29 December commemoration — and the backlash has begun.

body: The announcement came first; the backlash was never far behind. A day after Secretary to the Cabinet Patrick Kangwa confirmed that 18 October will no longer be observed as a public holiday, Reverend Godfridah Sumaili — the former National Guidance and Religious Affairs minister — condemned the decision as a betrayal.

body.text: The cancellation of the 18th October National Day of Prayer, Fasting and Reconciliation by government in consultation with some church mother bodies is a serious betrayal to Zambian Christian believers.
body.attribution: Reverend Godfridah Sumaili, quoted by Lusaka Times

body: Mr Kangwa's statement said the change followed consultations between the Government and the Church Mother Bodies. It revokes **Statutory Instrument No. 78 of 2015**, which made 18 October an annual public holiday, and replaces it with **Statutory Instrument No. 73 of 2026**, declaring 29 December a public holiday to be known as the National Day of Prayer and Christian Heritage. The first combined commemoration falls on 29 December this year.

Rev Sumaili rejected both the decision and the process. "We do not know who those church mother body leaders consulted, which is why Zambia's identity, values and aspirations have been taken away," she said, arguing the Government should have acted with the utmost responsibility on a matter of such public interest.

Her core objection is theological. The October day, she said, was a solemn occasion of repentance, fasting and seeking forgiveness, while 29 December celebrates the declaration of Zambia as a Christian nation. "I am wondering how a day of weeping and repentance could be combined with a day of celebration. This move shows a lack of spiritual understanding by those involved," she said, urging citizens to condemn the decision.

The Church Mother Bodies see it differently. In a joint statement on Thursday, carried by Mwebantu, they said the consolidation will strengthen the observance, placing it strategically between Christmas and New Year to allow wider participation. The statement that announced the change did not name the bodies consulted or detail what the merged commemoration will involve.

The merger formalises an announcement President Hichilema made in December 2025, at the 34th anniversary of the 1991 declaration of Zambia as a Christian nation by the late President Frederick Chiluba — that 29 December would become a permanent public holiday from 2026. The October day was itself created in 2015 under former President Edgar Lungu, after a call for national prayers over economic challenges, and has been marked annually with inter-denominational services at the Lusaka Showgrounds and across the country.

This year, 18 October falls on a Sunday. Zambians can still pray for the nation through regular church services, but it will otherwise be a normal day — and the official holiday now belongs to December.

sources.title: “Govt Has Betrayed Christians,” Sumaili Says As October 18 Holiday Ends
18th October, 2026 will not be observed as a Public Holiday says Government

stories.title: 'Incompetent': Sikota takes on the DPP over the treason-trial delay — as a constitutional petition gets October dates
stories.excerpt: Lead counsel Sakwiba Sikota says blaming investigations for the delay in bringing Brian Mundubile and 17 others to court is incompetent. Meanwhile a constitutional petition over the detentions has been scheduled for late October.

image.label: The waiting file
image.caption: The treason case, the sedition case and a constitutional petition now run on three separate calendars.

body: Sakwiba Sikota, lead counsel to Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu, has accused Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri of incompetence for justifying the delay in bringing the treason case to court when, he says, the matter has been under investigation for three years.

Mr Phiri had explained that complicated cases such as treason take time because of investigations, citing the 1985 Shamwana case, which he said took 11 months to commence. Mr Sikota, commenting in an interview on Thursday, rejected the comparison, News Diggers reports — pointing to the length of time the matter has already been under investigation.

Mr Mundubile, the NRPUP presidential candidate, his running mate Mr Zulu and 16 others were arrested and charged with treason in August and have been in detention since. The church and international bodies are among those who have called for a speedy trial. The treason charge itself has yet to reach a plea.

body.text: A second front: the constitutional petition

body: Separately, the High Court has scheduled the detainees' constitutional petition for hearing before a three-judge panel from **26 October to 6 November**, according to the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance, Zambian Eye reports. The petition, filed on 11 September, names Attorney General Harrington Akusanga and Zambia Correctional Service Commissioner General Fredrick Chilukutu as respondents, and invokes Articles 1, 13, 15 and 18 of the Constitution — challenging the arrests, the detention, transfers between facilities, and alleged restrictions on access to lawyers and family.

The alliance's acting secretary general, Muhabi Lungu, says the two leaders have spent 42 days in detention without appearing before a court on the treason allegations — a claim he frames as illegal detention, but which remains the alliance's position rather than any court's finding. Allegations in the petition of physical mistreatment and undisclosed holding locations likewise remain untested.

body.text: We just want to show that the State is ready to prosecute this case and deal with it in the most expeditious manner.
body.attribution: The prosecution, before the Solwezi Magistrate's Court on 5–6 October, quoted by Lusaka Times

body: The third calendar is Solwezi, where the pair face two counts of seditious practices under Section 57, read with Section 60, of the Penal Code. Principal Resident Magistrate Mambwe Mukonde has reserved to **Tuesday 13 October** her ruling on whether that court has jurisdiction — the defence argues the alleged offences were committed in Lusaka, and the State did not dispute that the warn-and-caution statements point to Lusaka. No plea has been taken. The defence has objected that the Solwezi venue "is merely intended to deprive us of easily accessing our witnesses"; the State says seven witnesses were ready at both sittings.

body.confirmed: Sikota publicly criticised the DPP's justification of the delay (News Diggers); the High Court petition is scheduled for 26 October–6 November per the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance (Zambian Eye); the Solwezi jurisdiction ruling is reserved to Tuesday 13 October (Lusaka Times, Times of Zambia). The 18 accused have been detained since August on treason charges.
body.unverified: The petition's allegations — mistreatment, undisclosed locations, restricted access to lawyers — have not been tested in court. The treason charges themselves have not been particularised in open court, and the accused have not taken plea.

sources.title: Sikota accuses DPP of incompetence over delayed Mundubile treason trial
Mundubile, Makebi constitutional rights petition set for October hearing
Mundubile, Makebi Want Sedition Trial Moved To Lusaka, Say Solwezi Venue Blocks Their Witnesses
Court rejects oral submissions in Mundubile case

stories.title: Forty thousand hires under the US health pact — and RDAZ says the queue should start with those already inside
stories.excerpt: The US$1.5 billion health memorandum signed on Thursday carries a plan to recruit 40,000 health workers over five years. The resident doctors say existing staff should come first; the opposition questions the deal itself.

image.label: The hiring plan
image.caption: The US health pact carries a plan to recruit 40,000 health workers over five years.

body: The health pact Zambia signed with the United States on Thursday has its first hard staffing number: **40,000 health workers over five years** — 15,000 frontline staff and 25,000 community health workers, according to the Times of Zambia.

Health Minister Professor Roma Chilengi described the US$1.5 billion Memorandum of Understanding as a monumental and landmark decision, saying it is meant to be a catalyst for self-sustainability and local financing that would enable the Government to employ the 40,000 over the five-year period. The US Embassy's Chargé d'Affaires, Mich Coker, said the MoU "represented a transformative partnership between the US and Zambia, one built on shared commitment and mutual accountability".

The Resident Doctors Association of Zambia says the recruitment should begin with those already in the system. In an interview on Friday, RDAZ president Dr Paul Chibwe said the Government needs to conduct a needs assessment, noting that promotions would create more vacancies in the sector, News Diggers reports.

The scepticism is sharper on the opposition benches. Democratic Progressive Party leader Antonio Mwanza questioned the excitement around the proposed recruitment, arguing that the Government can hire health workers without what he termed a questionable deal.

The pact has been this week's running story — negotiated for months, renegotiated after Zambia objected to data-sharing provisions, and signed on Thursday. The recruitment plan is the first detail of what it buys, and the argument over whose names go on the payroll has now begun in earnest.

For the doctors' association, the priority list is about retention as much as recruitment: hires made while existing staff wait for advancement risk feeding the very vacancies the programme is meant to close. For the Government, the five-year frame and the tapering US contribution are the point — the ministry's case is that the deal ends in Zambian self-reliance, not dependency.

sources.title: Prioritize those in the system in 40,000 health workers recruitment – RDAZ

stories.title: Ninety-first: the Chipolopolo slip a place in the FIFA rankings — even the Togo win could not hold 90th
stories.excerpt: Zambia have fallen one place to 91st in the FIFA/Coca-Cola World Ranking released on Wednesday, the 2-0 win over Togo outweighed by bigger gains elsewhere during the international window.

image.label: One place down
image.caption: Zambia slip to 91st in the FIFA world rankings despite beating Togo in the window.

body: Winning, it turns out, was not enough. Zambia have slipped one place to **91st** in the latest FIFA/Coca-Cola World Ranking, released on Wednesday 7 October, despite beating Togo 2-0 in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers during the window.

The Chipolopolo's tally now stands at 1,260.61 points. News Diggers reports that the victory over Togo earned a ten-point increment, leaving the total a marginal five points above where it stood before the window's two fixtures — against Algeria and Togo — but that the gain was insufficient to preserve 90th place as other nations made more significant strides.

The African pecking order is unchanged at the summit. Morocco continue to lead the continent and sit seventh globally with 1,805.34 points, followed by Senegal in 18th and Egypt in 25th. Zambia remain outside Africa's top ten, and the gap to the continent's leading pack is measured in hundreds of points.

Rankings mathematics are unforgiving in the middle of the table. A victory over a lower-rated opponent brings modest points, and a single place can turn on results played continents away; Zambia's window was profitable in points and still cost a rung.

The slip is a footnote rather than a crisis — World Cup and AFCON qualifying campaigns are settled on the pitch, not the rankings board, and seedings turn on sustained runs rather than single windows. But the October release is a reminder of how thin the margin for standing still has become: win, and you might still fall.

The next international window offers the next chance to convert points back into places — and the fixtures that matter most for the ranking are precisely the ones that matter most for the qualifying campaign.

sources.title: Zambia drops to 91st in FIFA rankings

stories.title: Eleven arrests at National Heroes Stadium: a fake cash-giveaway post drew a crowd — and a police warning on disinformation
stories.excerpt: Police arrested eleven people at National Heroes Stadium on Friday morning after a false social-media post promising free cash drew a crowd to Gate 1. Officers dispersed the gathering when it refused to leave.

image.label: The false post
image.caption: A false cash-giveaway post drew a crowd to National Heroes Stadium; eleven people were arrested.

body: A promise of free money that existed only on social media drew hundreds to National Heroes Stadium on Friday morning — and ended with eleven people under arrest and a public warning from the police about disinformation.

Matero Police Station received a report at about 07:30 hours that a large crowd had gathered at Gate 1 of the stadium, police spokesperson Godfrey Chilabi said. Officers who responded detained eleven people in connection with the incident; the Times of Zambia reports the suspects were caught compiling a list at the scene.

Preliminary investigations indicate the gathering followed a misleading post by an online commentator claiming that cash would be distributed at the stadium — a post that led many to believe they would each receive money.

body.text: Police officers engaged with the crowd and advised those present to disperse peacefully. When the crowd did not comply, officers dispersed it to maintain public order and ensure public safety.
body.attribution: Police spokesperson Godfrey Chilabi, in a statement reported by the Times of Zambia and Mwebantu

body: Mr Chilabi said investigations are ongoing and further updates will be provided. The Zambia Police Service urged the public to be wary of disinformation on social media — especially messages promising money or other benefits — and to verify such information with the authorities.
The situation at the stadium was calm by later in the day, with officers continuing to monitor the area.

body.confirmed: Eleven people were arrested at National Heroes Stadium on the morning of Friday 9 October after a crowd gathered over a false cash-giveaway post; police dispersed the crowd and opened investigations, per statements reported by the Times of Zambia and Mwebantu.
body.unverified: The identity of the online commentator behind the post, and whether anyone involved will face charges beyond the arrests themselves — police say investigations are ongoing.

sources.title: 11 Arrested at National Heroes Stadium Over Fake Cash Giveaway
Police disperse crowd at National Heroes Stadium over false cash giveaway

analysis.title: Staff-level is not signature: what the Fund's yes-in-principle actually buys
analysis.body:
A staff-level agreement is the Fund's negotiators saying the numbers add up — it is not the Fund's money. Between Friday's announcement and the first disbursement sit two gates: approval by IMF management and the Executive Board, and a set of prior actions Zambia must complete first. Neither the vote date nor the action list has been published.

The strongest reading for the Government is that the programme validates the stabilisation record — inflation back inside the target band at 6.1 percent, reserves near US$6.1 billion, growth projected at 5.6 percent — and locks in the pivot to growth before the 2027 budget is tabled. The strongest reading for sceptics is that the promises are the easy part: a primary surplus rising to 3 percent of GDP by 2029 means revenue measures and spending discipline that will be felt in every constituency, and the previous programme's goodwill was earned in the execution, not the announcement.

What to watch: the budget's arithmetic against the Fund's framework, and any movement on VAT-refund arrears and Food Reserve Agency oversight — the unglamorous items where programmes succeed or stall.

analysis.title: The unity call meets its first answer — and it comes with conditions
analysis.body:
The day after a presidential address is usually applause from one side and silence from the other. Saturday broke the pattern. Stephen Kampyongo, from the opposition benches, said the growth targets are reachable if Zambians embrace peace and unity — a conditional yes, but a yes. Britain's High Commissioner backed the Grow Zambia agenda in the same breath as insisting that opposition parties need room to operate and hold the Government accountable.

That pairing is the shape of the argument to come. The Government's strongest case is the one the President made himself: the election is over, the targets are national, and "the toxicity around here" — his own words — is a cost everyone pays. The critics' strongest case is that unity cannot be commanded from the podium while treason and sedition cases against election rivals grind through the courts, and that space for the opposition is measured in courtroom access, not closing speeches.

What to watch: the debate on the address in the House this week — the opposition's first formal reply — and Tuesday's Solwezi ruling, which will say as much about the political climate as any speech.

analysis.title: A Sunday in October: what moving the prayer day really changes
analysis.body:
Here is a detail worth pausing on: 18 October 2026 falls on a Sunday. For most workers, the practical difference this year is nil — the day was never going to be a working day anyway. What changed on Saturday is the calendar going forward, and the meaning attached to it.

The Government's case, through the Church Mother Bodies' joint statement, is consolidation: one stronger observance, placed between Christmas and New Year, marrying repentance to the celebration of the Christian-nation declaration. Reverend Sumaili's counter is that the two days are different spiritual acts — a day of weeping, as she puts it, cannot be merged with a day of celebration — and that the consultation behind the change is opaque. Both can be true at once: a tidier holiday calendar, and a genuine loss for those to whom 18 October's solemnity was the point.

What to watch: whether the merged 29 December commemoration draws the same breadth of participation the October day commanded, and whether the mother bodies name who they consulted — the absence of that detail is what gave the backlash its oxygen.
